US crime More than 35 woman come forward in case against fake 49ers player accused of fraud The FBI says Daejon Love and his alleged accomplice, Taylor Chan, defrauded women they met on dating apps out of $1.3m Uwa Ede-Osifo Fri 18 Sep 2026 21.37 EDT Last modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 21.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least 35 additional women have come forward with fraud allegations against Daejon Love , the man accused last month of masquerading as a San Francisco 49ers player and wealthy investor, the FBI announced on Friday. Federal authorities had previously said Love conned more than two dozen women, many of whom he met on dating apps, out of $1.3m. Love, 35, and alleged accomplice Taylor Chan, 18, who posed as his financial adviser, were arrested in August and have been charged with wire fraud. A public defender for Love and Chan’s attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Love allegedly used a combination of AI-assisted fake identities, fabricated investment accounts and staged video calls with Chan to gain the confidence of women in California, Idaho, Washington and Oregon, according to federal authorities. To some women, he claimed to be a former NFL player, to others he claimed he said he was on reserve or injured. Love convinced several women who believed they were dating him that if they sent him money for investments, it would yield high returns. The plot allegedly began around February 2022 up through the time of the pair’s arrest in August, according to prosecutors. Federal authorities have not publicly revealed how Love and Chan met. In court documents, prosecutors described Love as nomadic, saying little is known about his family ties and that he has no known legitimate source of employment. Since his arrest, texts and videos where Love flaunted a seemingly lavish lifestyle and 49ers paraphernalia have gone viral on social media, much to the amusement of some online users. At a Friday news conference, Portland FBI special agent Douglas Olson criticized any jokes levied at the women ensnared by Love’s scheme. “Victim blaming is unjust and it’s harmful and it overlooks the calculated, highly manipulative lengths these individuals went to deceive and exploit others,” Olson said. “Victims were encouraged to take out personal loans and make life altering financial decisions based on the belief they were building a future with someone they cared about. Once the money was taken, the victims were cut off, left without answers, without funds, and often without closure. Many lost not only their savings, but their sense of security and confidence,” he said. Olson urged any other potential victims to contact law enforcement. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Polymarket Polymarket temporarily suspends trading on international platform due to security incident Security incident linked to performance-monitoring tool spurred platform to halt trading for about an hour Associated Press Thu 29 Oct 2026 19.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international platform on Thursday because of a security incident that compromised a third-party provider, the company said. Trading was paused for about an hour and resumed on Thursday afternoon. The company has promised to fully reimburse any affected traders. Prediction markets surge in US as public health advocates call for support to combat gambling Read more The prediction market platform said it halted trading “out of an abundance of caution” after identifying and fixing the issue affecting its international platform. “We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders,” the company posted on X once trading had resumed. Polymarket said it referred the incident to a law enforcement agency in the United Kingdom. Reports have linked the source of the incident to DebugBear, a UK-based company offering website performance-monitoring tools. DebugBear’s own website was unavailable on Thursday afternoon and the company posted on X that it was “impacted by an ongoing security incident”. It also advised clients who were using one of its products to remove the embed code from their websites. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It was not immediately clear to what extent traders using the popular prediction market platform were affected, or the breadth of the impact. The company said anyone who was affected “will be made whole”.
